## Chapter summary {#data_in_R_summarySummary}


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| column: margin
#| fig-alt: "A close-up photograph of a vibrant pink *Clarkia xantiana* flower with delicate, deeply lobed petals. The petals have a soft gradient, fading from a rich pink at the center to a lighter shade towards the edges. The reproductive structures—dark purple stamens with pollen-covered anthers and a protruding stigma—are prominently visible. The background is softly blurred, showing additional flowers and green stems in what appears to be a greenhouse or controlled growth environment."
#| fig-cap: "A beautiful *Clarkia xantiana* flower."
include_graphics("../../figs/intro_to_r/data_in_R/pretty_stressed_clarkia.png")
```


By keeping data "tidy" (i.e. in a rectangle where each column represents a variable and each row represents an observation),  we can make use of the powerful tools of R's  [**tidyverse**](https://www.tidyverse.org/) approach. The [`dplyr`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/) package is our first step into the tidyverse. [`dplyr`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/)  offers a numerous usefull functions for transforming and analyzing data, including:   

- [`mutate()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/mutate.html) for adding or modifying columns.      
 
- [`select()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/select.html) for choosing columns.    
- [`filter()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/filter.html) for subsetting rows,   and    
- [`rename()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/rename.html) for changing column names.  

Together (and when combined with the pipe operator, `|>`) these tools allow us to get a lot done in R. In the next three chapters we learn how to use R to summarize single variable, and associations between variables in R. Thus we are well on our way, to being able to (1) load (2) visualize (3) work with, and (4) summarize data reprodicbly in R. WOohooHOO!.

### Practice Questions {#data_in_R_summaryPractice_questions} 


Try these questions! 


:::exercises


**Q1)** Consider the table below. The data are `r mcq(c("tidy", answer = "not tidy"))`


```{r, echo=FALSE}
head(ril_data)|> select(location, ril, mean_visits) |> t()|>kable()
```


`r hide("Click here for explanation")`

Here the data are transposed, so the data are not tidy. Remember in tidy data each variable is a column, not a row. This is particularly hard for R because there are numerous types of data in a column. 

`r unhide()`. 

--- 


**Q2)** Consider the table below. The data are `r mcq(c("tidy",  answer ="not tidy"))`


```{r, echo=FALSE}
head(ril_data)|> select(location, ril, mean_visits) |> mutate(`location-ril` = paste(location,ril, sep = "-"))|> dplyr::select(`location-ril`, mean_visits) |>kable()
```


`r hide("Click here for explanation")`

Here location and ril are combined in a single column, so the data are not tidy. Remember in tidy data each variable is its own  column. It would be hard to get e.g. means for RILs of locations in this format.  

`r unhide()`

--- 




**Q3)** Consider the table below. The data are `r mcq(c("tidy", answer = "not tidy"))`


```{r, echo=FALSE}
(bind_rows(head(ril_data), head(ril_data|> filter(location=="SR"), n=6) ))|> 
  filter(location =="SR"|location == "GC")|>
  select(location, ril, mean_visits) |> pivot_wider(id_cols = ril, names_from = location, values_from = mean_visits)|>kable()
```



`r hide("Click here for explanation")`

This is known as "wide format" and is not tidy. Here the variable, location,  is used as a column heading. This can be a fine way to present data to people, but it's not how we are analyzing data.   

`r unhide()`


--- 

**Q4)** You should always make sure data are tidy when (pick best answer) `r longmcq(c("collecting data", "presenting data",answer = "analyzing data with dplyr",  "all of the above"))`
:::

**Q5)** Consider the table above and code below. What is the value of `pl_pw_ratio` in the first row? `r fitb(num=TRUE, answer = 7)`

iris |> 
  mutate(pl_pw_ratio = Petal.Length / Petal.Width)

---

**Q6)** Consider the code below. Which  column names will appear in the output? (select all that apply). `r longmcq(c("Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width",  "Petal.Length", "Petal.Width", answer =   "Species", answer = "pl_pw_ratio"))`

```{r}
#| eval: false
iris |> 
  mutate(pl_pw_ratio = Petal.Length / Petal.Width) |>
  select(Species, pl_pw_ratio)
```

---

**Q7)** Say I wanted to use clean_names() from janitor. Which two of the scripts below would work? `r mcq(c("A and B","A and C","A and D",answer = "B and C","B and D","C and D"))`

```{r}
#| eval: false
# A
iris |> 
  clean_names() |>
  mutate(pl_pw_ratio = Petal.Length / Petal.Width)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
# B
iris |> 
  mutate(pl_pw_ratio = Petal.Length / Petal.Width)|>
  clean_names() 
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
# C
iris |> 
  clean_names()  |>
  mutate(pl_pw_ratio = petal_length / petal_width)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
# D
iris |> 
  clean_names()  |>
  mutate(pl_pw_ratio = Petal.Length / Petal.Width)
```

**Use the R environment below to answer the next set of questions**   


```{webr-r}
#| context: setup
library(dplyr)
library(conflicted)
conflicts_prefer(stats::filter)
iris$Species <- as.character(iris$Species) 
iris <- tibble(iris)
```  

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true
library(conflicted)
library(dplyr)

iris |>  
  filter(Species == "setosa")
```  


:::exercises


**As you can see, the code above returns the error: \"Error: object 'Species' not found.\"** 

**Q8)** What was this code aiming to do? `r longmcq(c("Create a new column called Species","Convert Species to a factor", answer = "Return only the rows of the iris dataset where Species is \"setosa\"","Remove the Species column from the dataset", "Sort the dataset by Species"))`

---  

**Q9)** Why did the error, \"Error: object 'Species' not found.\" arise? `r longmcq(c("We use select() to select by values in a row, not filter()",  "The iris dataset does not contain a Species column","The Species column was deleted in the setup chunk", "filter() only works on tibbles, not data frames", "Species must be quoted inside filter()" ,   answer = "R used stats::filter() instead of dplyr::filter(), so Species was looked for as an object (not a column)"))`

`r hide("HINT")`
Try typing `glimpse(iris)`
`r unhide()`

---

**Q10)** How to fix the error  \"Error: object 'Species' not found.\"? Find both correct answers `
`r longmcq(c("Convert iris to a tibble first:</br><code>as_tibble(iris) |> filter(Species == \"setosa\")</code></br></br>",  answer = "Tell R to use dplyr's filter:</br><code>iris|>dplyr::filter(Species == \"setosa\")</code></br></br>", "Rename species to Species:</br><code> iris|>rename(Species=species)|>filter(Species==\"setosa\")</code></br></br>", "Filter on species, not Species:</br><code>iris|>filter(species == \"setosa\")</code></br></br>",answer = "Tell R to use dplyr's filter. After library(dplyr), type:</br><code>conflicts_prefer(dplyr::filter)</code></br></br> "))`



`r hide("Reveal: Why did this happen?")`

**Debugger’s note:** In a hidden setup chunk I wrote: `conflicts_prefer(dplyr::filter)` to tell R to prefer `stats::filter()` over `dplyr::filter()`.  Because of this, `filter()` no longer understands column names inside a data frame. So I forced this error on you.

In real workflows, it can be hard to predict which version of a function R will use.  This issue arises even when I don't trick you. So always tell R which version of filter() you want to use. `filter()` may on your computer today without `dplyr::filter()` or `conflicts_prefer(dplyr::filter)`, but it might not work on someone else computer (it might even fail on your computer next week).

`r unhide()`
:::





### Glossary of Terms  {#data_in_R_summaryGlossary_of_terms} 

:::glossary


- **Tidy Data**   A structured format where:  
   - Each **row** represents an **observation**.  
   - Each **column** represents a **variable**.  
   - Each **cell** contains a **single measurement**.    

- **Tibbles:**  A modern form of a **data frame** in R with:   
   - Cleaner printing (only first 10 rows, fits columns to screen).  
   - Explicit display of **data types** (e.g., <dbl>, <chr>).  
   - Strict subsetting (prevents automatic type conversion).  
   - Character data is **not automatically converted to factors**.   

- **Piping (|>) functions:**  A way to **chain operations together**, making code more readable and modular.    
- **Missing Data (`NA`):** R uses `NA` to represent missing values.   Operations with `NA` return `NA` unless handled explicitly (e.g., na.rm = TRUE to ignore missing values, use = \"pairwise.complete.obs\", etc).     
- **Warnings**: Indicate a possible issue but allow code to run (e.g., NAs introduced by coercion).     
- **Errors**: Stop execution completely when something is **invalid**.  



:::

---

### Key R functions  {#data_in_R_summaryNew_r_functions}  


:::functions


- **[`read_csv()`](https://readr.tidyverse.org/reference/read_delim.html)** *([readr](https://readr.tidyverse.org/))*: Reads a CSV file into R as a **tibble**, automatically guessing column types.  

- **[`select()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/select.html)** *([dplyr](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/))*: Selects specific columns from a dataset.  

- **[`mutate()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/mutate.html)** *([dplyr](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/))*: Creates or modifies columns in a dataset.  

- **[`dplyr::filter()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/filter.html)** *([dplyr](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/). Because there is a different filter in a different package, always specify which filter you want r to use.)*: Only retains rows which meet some logical criteria.   


- **[`rename()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/rename.html)** *([dplyr](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/)*: Allows you to manually changes column names.   

- **[`as.numeric()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/numeric.html)**: Converts a vector to a numeric data type.  


- **[`|>`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/programming.html)** *([Base R Pipe Operator](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/pipe.html))*: Passes the result of one function into another, making code more readable.  


:::

---



### R Packages Introduced {#data_in_R_summaryR_packages_introduced}  


:::packages


- **[`readr`](https://readr.tidyverse.org/)**: A tidyverse package for reading rectangular data files (e.g., `read_csv()`).

- **[`dplyr`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/)**: A tidyverse package for data manipulation, including `mutate()`, `glimpse()`, and `across()`.  

:::
